I’m using a Canon imagePROGRAF PRO‑300 inkjet with Avery Durable White Film labels, and this combination is designed for professional, long-lasting, archival results. The PRO‑300 uses Canon’s LUCIA PRO pigment inks, which are very different from the dye inks in most consumer inkjets. Pigment inks contain extremely tiny solid particles that sit on the surface of the label and bond with the coating, making them highly resistant to fading, water, and UV light. Dye inks, by contrast, soak into the surface and are prone to smearing and fading over time. The Avery Durable White Film labels are made of a tough polyester material which is marketed as tear-resistant, water-resistant, oil-resistant, scuff-resistant, and fade-resistant, making them far more durable than paper labels. They’re also coated for inkjet use, allowing the pigment ink to adhere properly. Together, this setup should produce labels with longevity and durability that is comparable or exceeds laser printing.  Also, the Canon PRO‑300 with its 10 ink cartridges produces far superior print quality to a laser printer, with richer colors, smoother gradients, and sharper detail, especially on coated film labels.

I also really like the look of pearlized labels. However, despite numerous attempts, I wasn’t able to dial in the color and ink settings for the PRO‑300 to get satisfactory results, and the laser print quality on them is noticeably inferior to the inkjet. The pearlized labels also do not have the longevity of the film labels, but if the cartridges are kept in the game box they should last for decades. The original Bally cartridge labels appear to have been printed on paper using offset lithography and oil-based pigment inks.  Most of my cartridges which I've always kept in the Astrocade top storage compartment still look okay, although they are a little faded and have some foxing.

The glossy labels also look great with the white background sticker.  They are paper labels and work well with the Pro-300.

I'll post some more pics later today of the labels on the actual cartridges.

New Image

22291:
Steps 1 and 2.  
Check for clock signal and voltages.
Likely culprits in the oscillator area are U16 and the crystal, unless you have a U32 chip and not a kludge board, which is kind of rare.
Pin 1 on any RAM - negative 5 voltsPin 8 on any RAM - 12 or 15 volts
Pin 9 on any RAM - 5 volts
Pin 40 on the address chip (center of the 3 customs) - 10 volts

If those are all good, 9 times out of 10 it's just a bad RAM.  The hard part can be figuring out which one.  I have a diagnostic tool that will zero in on which one is bad.
I've found more bad Z-80's than bad custom chips (but not by much), so check signals there as well.  A failed custom chip is not as common as the internet would have you believe.

value but also pitfalls and grey area of generative AI (which before the

learning, LLM and neural networks). A committee was formed to evaluate
individual use cases and to vet particular AI products and integrations. The
stance was initially "no" to any AI, but it did not take long to realize
that in the month of reviewing a single AI candidate, a dozen more had
popped up and seemingly overnight every single piece of software from Office
365, to Adobe, to Visual Studio and all the search engines had introduced
obsessive AI integrations whether we wanted them or not. Effectively, there
is no escaping this now.

overtaking every social platform and sector of creativity. I can no longer
even browse Facebook without refining my feed to show only content from
those I follow (which Zuckerberg cleverly reverts again every time you
refresh). Every other suggested post is just another AI content farm pushing
out fake imagery with a made-up story and bot responses, which in turn lead
to heightened engagement on the platform and real users then begin reacting
with many not realizing it is all imagined content. You'd be amazed to find
out just how many 125 year olds have to bake their own cakes and nobody even
gives them one like on Facebook until encouraged by the bot posts (sarcasm).

"content creators" to monetize it, so suddenly it is just a rush to make
shovelware garbage content for likes and clicks. Meta even started pushing
out their own AI avatars to infiltrate their platforms, while embedding
tools to groups and pages to randomly post "engaging" topics via AI
language. It has made the platform largely unusable for me.

erroneous AI-generated facts using AI videos that at one point has a man

at another moment a vague CRT-looking device depicts the Bally library by
showing "The Inriribbhe Wizzland" It is toxic. Searching information on

itself is often riddled with errors as it uses sources that themselves are

with many sites including personal blogs and information sites finding their

That's my opinion in general about AI and my disappointment in how it has

This is off-topic from the original Lootera thread, but I thought it might be of interest to anyone looking to bring the Astrocade to events without the 5-minute screen shutoff.

In theory, you could build a small “keep-awake” adapter for the rear expansion that talks directly to the Z80 bus and, every 10 to 30 seconds, performs a valid RAM write to refresh the Astrocade’s idle timer. The BIOS uses a timeout byte at $4FEC (TIMOUT) that is decremented once per second; when it reaches 0 the screen blanks.

The dongle briefly requests the bus by pulling /BUSREQ low and waiting for /BUSACK low (CPU tri-states), then drives A0–A15 = $4FEC and D0–D7 = $FF, pulses /MREQ and /WR low to store $FF at $4FEC, releases all lines, and lets /BUSREQ return high. The operation takes microseconds, is repeated infrequently, and injects no fake inputs, so menus and games are unaffected. Keep all outputs tri-stated except during the BUSREQ window, use proper 5 V tolerant bus transceivers, include a front-panel enable switch, and you have a clean hardware screen-blanking blocker that is invisible to software.

Even better add some RAM and it could double as a memory expansion.

Hopefully, one of the members with more hardware experience could confirm if this is a valid approach.

Just to clarify some of the differences between the 2 BASIC's here are some notable changes:

1) All of the music designators have changed. The original (I'll just call it Bally and the other Astro) uses direct port calls like &(16), &(15) etc. and the Astro uses 2 byte references like VA, VB, etc. That is why the sound comes out garbled. If you chang all of those, your sound will be OK. 
2) The speed for inputting a file from tape (or computer) is greatly increased in Astro. The baud rate is 2000 bytes/s as opposed to 300 bytes/s.
3) The access to the color ports is similar to the sound ports.
4) The Astro has e new way for the string memory to be accessed. The Bally uses just the @()  string, which starts it's memory from the 1byte after the last byte in the BASIC program and works down to the last byte of free space. The Astro also uses this string, but also has the *()string. That starts from the last byte of available memory and works toward the end of the program. The main problem with the Bally version is that if you modify the code and already have something stored in the @() string, you move the entire string by that many bytes. if you delete are add, either way, you will lose the association of the string to what you have in it.I personally like the *() string.
5) The Bally need the extra hardware, the cassette interface to get information to/from a tape or computer, but the Astro has it's own built in interface.
These are the main differences I cam remember off the top of my head, which at 78 YO is starting to not remember as much as I could back when I started using the Bally BASIC in 1982.  OMG that's 43 years ago!!!!

The Pits
By Rex Goulding
ARCADIAN 3, no. 10 (Aug. 12, 1981): 108.

"The Pits" is one of my favorite games for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade with Bally BASIC or "AstroBASIC."  On December 16, 2019, I noticed that "placelogohere" made a gameplay video of the game and posted it to YouTube on September 16, 2017.  As of yesterday, two years later, I was only the second person to watch the video.  What a shame!  I thought it would be a good idea to make a gameplay video of "The Pits" with some explanation of the game; thus I created this video.

This isn't the first time that I've tried to shine a spotlight onto "The Pits" to give it some well-deserved attention.  In Episode 4 (August 2016) of the Bally Alley Astrocast, I covered this game with Chris (the podcast's co-host).  You can listen to that podcast here:

https://ballyalleyastrocast.libsyn.com/podcast/bally-alley-astrocast-004-sea-devil-and-the-pits

The object of "The Pits" is to move the small dot in the upper-left corner past the pits to the center of the medium-size box in the lower-right corner.  The clunker is that the pits move up the screen all the time and can catch you.  Each time the screen rolls up it counts as one move.  A successful trip in 16 moves is doing well.  This BASIC game is available for Bally BASIC and "AstroBASIC" and can be downloaded from BallyAlley.com.

"The Pits" is a perfect example that gameplay is the true measure of a game's value and that graphics can be completely secondary to the core gameplay experience.

----------

I have also attached a commented version of the Bally BASIC version of the BASIC listing for "The Pits" which I made in 2016.  I don't think that I have shared it with the public before now.  Maybe this is the motivation Chris needs to convert this game, eh, Chris?

There is thread that was originally posted in March of 2011 to the Yahoo group (now it's on groups.io) called "'The Pits' for AstroBASIC - A FANTASTIC Game!'"  You can read it here:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/54296158#msg10467

The game can be downloaded in AstroBASIC format here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_i-p/pits,_the_%5Brex_goulding%5D.zip

The game is also available in Bally BASIC.  This is probably the preferable version to play.  It is here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_i-p/programs_i-p.html#ThePitsRexGouldingBB

You can load and play it in the MAME emulator or on real hardware as a tape.

In 2011, "The Pits" was converted to an 8K BASICart ROM image, a homebrew cartridge that holds a BASIC program and a modified version of AstroBASIC.  The person who made this cartridge version of "The Pits" (I think it was Richard Degler) asked for it not to be distributed, so it's not available.  Plus, he asked me to delete the file, so I think it's gone off my hard drive too.

Now that I'm thinking about "The Pits" and its conversion to a BASICart, I think that Richard Degler converted about thirty AstroBASIC programs to cartridges.  On August 09, 2012, he asked Paul Thacker, Lance Squire and me to delete the files that he had sent to us to test.

If you haven't played "The Pits" yet, then give it whirl; you will like it.

They were well-received and introduced new folks to the platform for the first time, including the event organizer. Rather than adhering to the structured challenge where it’s all about byte compression, I love using Bally to get creative with the theme. Even so it clocks in at just 300 bytes and I could easily imagine this as a type-in from a holiday edition newsletter back in the day 😊

Standout enhancements for me include the small and large font capabilities to squeeze way more code on screen at once while still remaining legible. I was curious why the Astrocade, and the MAME emulator as well, always show a purple vertical line along the right edge of the game menu screen. I assume the line was not intentional.

After digging into the BIOS source code, I found a small bug in the system power-up routine. During startup, the UPI routine SETOUT is called with a horizontal color boundary value of *41* , but the correct value should be *42*.

Here is why that matters.

The horizontal color boundary controls how color is applied across the screen, measured in blocks of 4 pixels. The effective range is 0 to 42. The Astrocade screen RAM has *40 bytes per row* , and since the system uses 2-bit color, each byte represents *4 pixels*. That gives a visible resolution of *160 pixels* across.

In addition to the useable screen area, the hardware adds a fixed frame on both the left and right sides. Each side is *2 bytes wide* , or *8 pixels*. You cannot draw into the frame, but you can choose which of the four system colors the frame uses.

Here is the odd part: the hardware includes the *right-side frame* in the horizontal color boundary calculation, but not the left side. So, the total horizontal range becomes:

*40* bytes of screen RAM + *2* bytes of right-side frame = *42*

Because of this, the boundary really needs to be set to 42, not 41 in order to only use the left side colors.

There is one more detail that explains the purple line itself. To save ROM space, the power-up routine defines only a *4-byte color table* called MENUCL. However, the routine COLSET expects *8 bytes* : 4 for the left side and 4 for the right side. Since only 4 bytes are provided, it simply keeps reading whatever data comes next in memory.

Immediately following MENUCL in the BIOS is:

DB $FF JP RVECT3

Which assembles to:

$FF $C3 $0D $20

Because the frame color defaults to column 0, which is processed last, the right-side frame ends up using $20 for one 4-pixel block. On the Astrocade, $20 corresponds to purple, which explains the vertical purple line.

This is just an academic curiosity. I am not suggesting anyone fix it. But it is a neat example of how a tiny off-by-one value and a few bytes of adjacent code can create a visible artifact that survives all the way into modern emulation.  Here are pics of the original and my patched BIOS.

I have a Seawolf Videocade where the TV vertical split line is NOT off to the right of the screen, displaying an annoying pink color 00 along the right side of the TV display.

I copied the Seawolf program to an EEPROM and moved the split line off the screen by 2 bytes. I use this EEPROM on a multi-carted cartridge with a ZIF socket. Moving the pink color off the screen makes playing that game so much more visually appealing.

I would like to add a little more info to Ryland Dagger's cool posting relating to the Astrocade BIOS power up routine.

The vertical TV display's split line initializes (powers on) all the way to the left of the screen RAM area (bits 0-5 of output port 09H = zero).

The vertical blanking line (output port 0AH) initializes (powers on) in location zero which is the very top of the screen RAM area.

Pixel colors are initialized at power on to zero (black).

The power up routine in the low-res ROM attempts to set up these 2 output ports 09 and 0AH using a UPI subroutine which utilizes a Z80 stack area in the bottom of the screen RAM area.

If the motherboard screen RAM has an operation issue, the UPI screen set up subroutine won't execute.

This is why a screen RAM issue is typically notorious for powering on with the dreaded "black screen" instead of scrambled graphic colors. The blanking line initially zero'd, hides all the pixels in the screen RAM area.

A short simple machine language (ML) TV screen set up program located at 2000H with a Z80 Jump instruction (opcode C3 x x), where C3 is at 2000H, can increase the chances of getting some kind of a color power on, as opposed to a black screen because the cartridge program can utilize direct ML instructions to set up the various TV screen parameters without utilizing a subroutine, which requires a no issue operating Z80 stack.

This is why I created the SetScreen power on diagnostic which is archived on the Bally Alley. You can end the simple screen set up program at 2000H with a Z80 halt instruction (opcode 76H) and the Z80 CPU will go into a halt mode executing NOPs nonstop (unless you press the reset button).

With just a simple logic probe, you can check for some inactive or bad signal lines.

You can also use this ML set up program and a logic probe, when the motherboard is working perfect, to note what is normal activity when the Z80 is halted. For example, you can note normal activities for the various motherboard clocks, the 3 screen RAM control lines and even confirm the Z80 is actually halted (Z80 pin 18).

This troubleshooting approach is not a substitute for having access to the diagnostic programs Z80 Check and Balcheck but it can be helpful at times to help isolate a failure on the motherboard.

I use the K and H products LP-3500 logic probe.

The low-res power on routine looks for 2 sentries at 2000H, C3 or 55H and responds accordingly.
If C3, jump to 2000H.
If 55, continue and display a menu using a linked list (table) within the cartridge ROM. The Nutting Manual provides info relating to the low-res Menu.
